body.objective: Students will be able to define sustainability.
successCriteria: I can define sustainability and its three pillars
I can tell sustainable from unsustainable practices
I can apply sustainability thinking to everyday choices
body.hook: Imagine a bank account where you only spend the interest and never touch the savings: it lasts forever. Sustainability is the same idea for the planet: living off nature's "interest" without using up the "savings."

vocabulary.definition: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
A resource that can be replaced naturally, such as forests, fish or sunlight.
A resource that can't be replaced in a human lifetime, such as oil, coal or minerals.
Careful use and protection of resources.
The largest population an environment can support long-term.

study.title: Living Off the Interest
study.question: What does sustainability mean, and how can we live sustainably?
study.passage:
Key ideas (written for this lesson):
Definition: the 1987 Brundtland Report (Our Common Future) defined sustainable development as development that "meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs."
Three pillars: environmental (healthy ecosystems), social (fair, healthy communities), economic (jobs and stable livelihoods). A sustainable choice balances all three.
Renewable resources are only sustainable if used no faster than they renew (e.g. fishing less than fish reproduce, harvesting forests within regrowth rates).
Fishing game: groups share a "lake" of 20 fish crackers; each round, each person may catch fish; after each round the remaining fish double (to a maximum of 20). Groups that overfish run out. Discuss: what rules made the lake last?
Everyday sort: classify practices as sustainable or not and explain with the three pillars (reusable bottles, fast fashion, local food, idling cars, repairing electronics, single-use packaging).
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; definition from the 1987 Brundtland Report.
steps: Discuss rules that made the lake last
discussion: What happened to the lake in your group?
How is the fishing game like real fisheries?
Which everyday change could you make?
study.product: Write a paragraph explaining sustainability using the fishing game and one everyday example, referring to all three pillars.

body.objective: Students will be able to analyze how climate affects local ecosystems.
body.iCan: I can analyze how climate affects local ecosystems.
successCriteria: I can explain the difference between weather and climate
I can describe how climate change affects Alberta ecosystems
I can analyze climate data and draw conclusions
body.hook: Alberta's glaciers are shrinking, spring arrives earlier, and insects like the mountain pine beetle now survive winters that once killed them. Climate shapes every ecosystem, and when it changes, ecosystems change too.

vocabulary.definition: Short-term conditions of the atmosphere, such as today's temperature.
The average weather of a place over 30 years or more.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide or methane, that traps heat in the atmosphere.
A large, slow-moving mass of ice formed from compacted snow.
When species move to new areas as conditions change.
The timing of seasonal events, like flowering or migration.

study.title: Climate and Our Ecosystems
study.question: How does changing climate affect Alberta ecosystems?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
Weather vs climate: a cold January day is weather; Alberta's average January temperature over 30 years is climate.
Greenhouse gases trap heat; burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide, and global average temperatures have risen since the late 1800s.
Alberta examples: the Athabasca Glacier in Jasper National Park has retreated by more than a kilometre since the late 1800s; markers along the trail show where the ice once reached. Mountain glaciers and snowpack feed rivers through summer, so their loss affects water supply. The mountain pine beetle spread across Alberta's forests partly because winters cold enough to kill the larvae became less common. Earlier springs can shift phenology: plants may flower before their pollinators are active. Warmer, drier conditions can increase wildfire risk.
Data activity: groups get a table of average temperatures for an Alberta city by decade (teacher provides from Environment and Climate Change Canada's historical data) and a table of a glacier's terminus positions. Graph them, describe the trend, and connect it to an ecosystem effect.
study.source: Summary from public sources such as Parks Canada and Environment and Climate Change Canada; teachers provide current data tables.
discussion: What trend did your graph show?
How could glacier loss affect prairie rivers?
Why did warmer winters help the pine beetle?
What is one effect of earlier springs?
study.product: Create a graph of an Alberta climate dataset, describe the trend and explain one effect on an Alberta ecosystem.

body.objective: Students will be able to calculate an ecological footprint.
body.iCan: I can calculate an ecological footprint.
successCriteria: I can explain what an ecological footprint measures
I can calculate and analyze my own footprint
I can set realistic goals to reduce my footprint
body.hook: If everyone on Earth lived like the average Canadian, we would need several planets' worth of resources. An ecological footprint calculator shows where your own impact comes from and where you could shrink it.

vocabulary.definition: The area of land and water needed to supply what a person uses and absorb their waste.
A standard unit for measuring footprints and biocapacity.
The ability of ecosystems to produce resources and absorb waste.
The greenhouse gases produced by a person's or group's activities.
Using resources faster than nature can renew them.
The date each year when humanity has used up what Earth can renew in that year.

study.title: My Footprint
study.question: How big is my ecological footprint, and how can I reduce it?
study.passage:
Footprint activity (written for this lesson):
What it measures: the land and water needed for food, housing, transport, goods and services, and for absorbing carbon emissions, in global hectares. The Global Footprint Network compares this with Earth's biocapacity. When humanity's demand is greater, we are in overshoot; Earth Overshoot Day marks when the year's budget is used up. Canada's average footprint per person is among the highest in the world.
Calculate: use a reputable online footprint calculator (e.g. the Global Footprint Network's) or the teacher's paper version with questions on: food (meat, local, waste), home (size, heating, electricity), transport (car, bus, walking, flights), goods (new clothes, electronics, recycling).
Analyze: which category is largest? Compare with class averages (anonymous).
Goals: choose two realistic changes, estimate their effect with the calculator, and write SMART goals (e.g. "For four weeks, walk to school three days a week instead of being driven").
Fairness note: some choices depend on family circumstances and where you live; focus on what you can influence.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; concepts from the Global Footprint Network.
discussion: Which change had the biggest effect in the calculator?
Which changes are realistic for you?
Why do footprints differ between countries?
study.product: Report your footprint by category and write two SMART goals with estimated effects.
